candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls HTTP request parameter / form-field names and values (and equivalent WebFlux binding inputs). By using a field name that differs from the disallowed property only through a special Unicode case-mapping character, the attacker can make `DataBinder.isAllowed()` treat the field as allowed while `BeanWrapperImpl` still resolves it to the protected property.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The Javadoc states that disallowed-field matching is intended to be case-insensitive, so this bypass is contrary to the documented security contract rather than an intentional limitation. The bypass requires a configured disallowed-fields list; configurations that use only a narrow allowed-fields list are not bypassed by this path. `DirectFieldAccessor` does not have the first-character fallback, so direct-field-access binders are not affected in the same way. The unused `PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatchIgnoreCase()` helper is corroborating context, not proof; the concrete source-level mismatch between the two case-normalization strategies is the primary evidence.
candidates.impact: A security-relevant allow/deny control is bypassed: an attacker can bind fields explicitly listed as disallowed. Depending on the application's model, this can mean mass assignment of identifiers or authorization flags such as `id` or `isAdmin`, causing data-integrity or privilege-escalation impact. The issue affects both servlet and reactive binding paths because both use the same `DataBinder` checks.
candidates.prerequisites: An application uses Spring MVC/WebFlux data binding on a bean and relies on `DataBinder.setDisallowedFields(...)` (typically via `@InitBinder` or a `WebBindingInitializer`) instead of, or without a sufficiently narrow, allowed-fields list. The target property must be resolvable through the `CachedIntrospectionResults` first-character case fallback (default bean-property access; `DirectFieldAccessor` has no such fallback). The request parameter name must survive container decoding as the crafted Unicode string, which is normal for UTF-8 decoded query/form data.
candidates.root_cause: `DataBinder.isAllowed()` compares disallowed fields by lowercasing the request-supplied field with `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` and matching against disallowed patterns that were also lowercased with `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` (see `setDisallowedFields`). Bean property resolution, however, uses `CachedIntrospectionResults.getPropertyDescriptor()`, whose fallback calls `StringUtils.uncapitalize()` / `StringUtils.capitalize()`, which change the first character with `Character.toLowerCase()` / `Character.toUpperCase()`. For characters where full Unicode lowercasing differs from the single-character mapping (notably U+0130 `İ`, whose `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` form is `i` plus a combining dot), the field does not match the disallowed pattern but is still resolved by the property fallback to the real property (for example a property named `id` or `isAdmin`). The value is therefore applied despite the configured disallowed-field rule. The intended pattern-matching utility `PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatchIgnoreCase()` exists in this snapshot but has no callers, confirming that the case-insensitive comparison fix is absent from `DataBinder`.
candidates.title: DataBinder disallowedFields can be bypassed via inconsistent Unicode case handling
candidates.trace: 1. `ServletRequestDataBinder.bind(ServletRequest)` builds `MutablePropertyValues` from the request parameter names using `WebUtils.getParametersStartingWith()`; names are preserved without normalization. 2. `WebDataBinder.doBind` -> `DataBinder.doBind` -> `checkAllowedFields` canonicalizes each field name and calls `isAllowed(field)`. 3. For a crafted name whose `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` form does not equal the stored lowercased disallowed pattern, `isAllowed` returns true, so the property value is not removed. 4. `applyPropertyValues` delegates to `BeanWrapperImpl`; `CachedIntrospectionResults.getPropertyDescriptor()` first misses the exact crafted name, then falls back to `StringUtils.uncapitalize(name)`, which uses `Character.toLowerCase()` on the first character and can resolve the crafted name to the actual disallowed property. 5. The resolved setter is invoked, so the disallowed property is modified.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no runtime or test-suite confirmation was performed. Exact exploitability depends on the servlet container's UTF-8 parameter-name decoding and on the target bean having a property reachable through the first-character fallback. The repository snapshot contains no test sources and no commit metadata, so the precise upstream fix commit and any CVE/advisory mapping could not be verified from the assigned materials.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-178 Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity, leading to property injection / mass assignment (CWE-915)

coverage_summary: `get_source_scope` reported 4767 model-visible files, zero excluded for size, sensitive names/paths, or symlinks; the tree is Spring Framework 6.1.20-SNAPSHOT main sources plus build files, with no test sources present. I searched all modules for data-binding, allowed/disallowed field handling, case handling, and related web entry points; inspected the full `DataBinder`, `WebDataBinder`, `ServletRequestDataBinder`, `WebRequestDataBinder`, `WebExchangeDataBinder`, `CachedIntrospectionResults`, `StringUtils`, `PatternMatchUtils`, and functional resource-handling code; and sampled many other modules. Not every one of the 4767 files was read line-by-line.

No git history or commit metadata is available; the fix boundary and the meaning of the unused `simpleMatchIgnoreCase` helper are inferred from source and version/@since markers.
No external advisory, CVE, patch, or ground-truth lookup was permitted, and no code was executed.

Exact exploitability requires Java full-case-mapping semantics, UTF-8 request-parameter-name decoding, and a target bean property reachable through the first-character fallback; these were reasoned from source, not runtime-confirmed.
Only one candidate may be submitted under this review condition, so other plausible but weaker leads are listed only as rejected or unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: DataBinder constructor binding ignores allowed/disallowed fields
rejected_leads.reason: `DataBinder.createObject()` resolves constructor arguments without calling `isAllowed()`, but the same file's Javadoc repeatedly states that allowed/disallowed fields are not applicable to constructor binding via `construct`, and no source artifact ties this behavior to the case-handling defect. Treating it as an unconfirmed documented limitation rather than the selected candidate.

`PathResourceLookupFunction` in both WebMvc.fn and WebFlux.fn includes `processPath`, `isInvalidEncodedInputPath`, and `isResourceUnderLocation` checks. No clear bypass was identified in the inspected code.

The class filters read-only `ClassLoader`, `ProtectionDomain`, and non-owned `AutoCloseable` properties and restricts `Class`/`URL` introspection. No concrete bypass of those checks was found in the available source.

summary: Source scope is the Spring Framework 6.1.20-SNAPSHOT main-source tree (4767 model-visible files, no binary/sensitive/symlink exclusions; test sources are not present in this snapshot). The strongest candidate is a case-sensitivity bypass in `DataBinder`'s disallowed-fields protection: disallowed-field matching normalizes with `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`, while bean-property resolution uses `StringUtils.uncapitalize()`/`Character.toLowerCase()` for its fallback lookup. For characters where full Unicode lowercasing differs from the simple per-character mapping, notably U+0130 `İ`, a crafted request parameter can evade the disallowed-field pattern yet still resolve to the intended bean property, defeating `setDisallowedFields`. The 6.1.20 development line contains a new, currently unused `PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatchIgnoreCase()` helper, which is consistent with the missing use-site fix in `DataBinder.isAllowed()`. I found no stronger, better-evidenced issue in the reviewed areas.
